short: Fossil energy and mechanisation break the ceiling on economic growth.
full:
From around 1760, beginning in Britain, coal and steam replaced muscle, wind and water as the primary sources of usable power. Textiles mechanised first, then iron, then transport with railways and steamships. For the first time in history, output per person rose faster than population, and kept rising.

The social consequences were wrenching: mass urbanisation, factory discipline, child labour, and eventually trade unions, public health reform and mass literacy. A second wave from the 1870s added steel, chemicals, electricity and the internal combustion engine. The age also began the sustained rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide whose consequences define our own century.
